\vspace{0.3em}

This practice exam asks about the Counting Customers practice project. Exam 2
has the same format and asks the same kinds of question about your own
project, so work this one with your printed practice project in front of you.

80 minutes. 50 points. Paper notes only. No electronic devices.

# Part A: Inversion (8 points)

## Question 1 (1 point)

`rquit` takes the ceiling of $\log U / \log(1 - p)$. Without the ceiling,
what would it draw? Circle one.

1. An exponential with rate $-\log(1 - p)$.
1. The same geometric distribution.
1. The geometric distribution shifted down by one.
1. Negative values, since $\log U < 0$.

## Question 2 (1 point)

In Part A your QQ plot for $J$ has many points stacked at the same integer
heights, not a smooth line. Does this mean the sampler is wrong? Circle one.

1. No. Both sets of quantiles are integers, so many points coincide. The
   check is whether they sit on the 45 degree line.
1. Yes. A correct sampler gives a smooth line.
1. Yes. Discrete variables cannot be checked with a QQ plot.
1. No, but only because 10,000 draws is a large sample.

## Question 3 (6 points)

**(i)** (2 points) Show that if $E$ is exponential with rate $-\log(1 - p)$,
then $\lceil E \rceil$ has the distribution of $J$. Hint: find
$P(\lceil E \rceil > j)$.

\vspace{1.5in}

\newpage

**(ii)** (2 points) Suppose in Part A you had compared your draws with
`qgeom(u, p)`, without the $+1$. Describe what the QQ plot would show, and
what you would conclude from it.

\vspace{1.3in}

**(iii)** (2 points) Part A checked your sampler against `qgeom`, which R
provides. Describe two ways to check a sampler for a
distribution R has no functions for at all.

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

# Part B: Mixtures (8 points)

## Question 4 (1 point)

In Part B you drew $p$ and then $J \mid p$. What kind of construction
is the distribution of $J$? Circle one.

1. A mixture, with a random parameter $p$.
1. A sum of independent geometric variables.
1. A convolution of a beta and a geometric, $p + J$.
1. A transformation $J = h(p)$ for a fixed function $h$.

## Question 5 (1 point)

In Part B the mean of your 10,000 draws of $J$ was about 195, and the
largest was over 330,000. You rerun with 1,000,000 draws. What happens to the sample
mean? Circle one.

1. It does not settle down. It tends to be larger, and depends on the few
   largest draws.
1. It settles near 195.
1. It settles near $1/\E{p} = (a + b)/a \approx 4$.
1. It settles near $\E{1/p}$, a finite number.

## Question 6 (6 points)

**(i)** (2 points) If every customer had the average quitting probability
$a/(a + b) \approx 0.25$, the chance of staying past 100 purchases would be
$0.75^{100} \approx 5 \times 10^{-13}$. Part B found $P(J > 100) \approx 0.05$.
Explain why letting $p$ vary across customers makes long stays so much more
likely.

\vspace{1.5in}

\newpage

**(ii)** (2 points) Given $p$, $\E{J \mid p} = 1/p$. Show that
$\E{J} = \E{1/p}$ is infinite when $p \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)$ with $a < 1$.
Hint: look at the integral near $p = 0$.

\vspace{1.5in}

**(iii)** (2 points) Part B checked the tail $P(J > j)$ at $j = 1$, 10 and 100
against the formula, and did not compare the sample mean with anything. Why
is the mean useless as a check here, and why do the tail probabilities work?

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

# Part C: Accept-reject (8 points)

## Question 7 (1 point)

In Part C a candidate $Y$ is accepted when $U \le (1 - Y)^{b - 1}$. Which
candidates are most likely to be rejected? Circle one.

1. Candidates near 1.
1. Candidates near 0.
1. Candidates near the mode of $f$.
1. None. Every candidate has the same chance.

## Question 8 (1 point)

Could importance resampling with the same candidate density
$g(p) = a p^{a - 1}$ have drawn from the Beta in Part C? Circle one.

1. Yes. $g$ is positive wherever $f$ is, and the weights $f/g$ are bounded.
1. No. Importance resampling needs uniform candidates.
1. No. Importance resampling needs the normalizing constant $B(a, b)$.
1. No. $f$ is unbounded near 0.

## Question 9 (6 points)

**(i)** (2 points) In Part C you accepted 4,759 of 10,000 candidates, with a
95\% interval of $(0.466, 0.486)$, against $1/c = a B(a, b) \approx 0.475$.
Is the difference between 0.476 and 0.475 a sign of a problem? What would a
problem look like?

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

**(ii)** (2 points) Suppose $b$ had been 0.5 instead of 2.426, with $a$
unchanged. Does the bound on $f/g$ in Part C still hold? What goes wrong, and what
kind of candidate density might work instead?

\vspace{1.5in}

**(iii)** (2 points) Part C drew the Beta by accept-reject but drew the
candidate $g$ by inversion. Why is inversion the natural choice for $g$ but
not for the Beta?

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

# Part D: The purchase process (8 points)

## Question 10 (1 point)

`purchases` draws each purchase time from the one before it. Which
factorization of the joint distribution of the purchase times does this use?
Circle one.

1. $f(t_1) f(t_2 \mid t_1) f(t_3 \mid t_2) \cdots$, each time depending only
   on the one before.
1. $f(t_1) f(t_2) f(t_3) \cdots$, since the times are independent.
1. $f(t_1 \mid t_2, t_3, \ldots) f(t_2 \mid t_3, \ldots) \cdots$, starting
   from the last purchase.
1. None. The times are drawn together as a vector.

## Question 11 (1 point)

Your simulated data set in Part D had 1,386 customers with no repeat
purchase, and the real data has 1,411. What would tell you whether a gap this
size is a problem? Circle one.

1. Repeat the simulation many times and see whether 1,411 falls in the
   middle 95\% of the simulated counts.
1. A $t$-test comparing the simulated and real counts of repeat purchases.
1. One simulation with ten times as many customers.
1. Nothing. Any gap means the model is wrong.

## Question 12 (6 points)

**(i)** (2 points) Over $t$ weeks an active customer's number of purchases
is Poisson($\lambda t$), which R can draw in one call. Why does `purchases`
draw the gaps one at a time instead?

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

**(ii)** (2 points) Suppose you repeated the Part D simulation 100 times and
took the middle 95\% of the number of customers with no repeat purchase. This
treats the paper's $r$, $\alpha$, $a$ and $b$ as the truth, but they are
estimates from these same 2,357 customers. Would the range be wider or
narrower if it allowed for that? Explain.

\vspace{1.3in}

**(iii)** (2 points) Your Part D table matched the real counts of repeat
purchases closely. Name one thing the model claims about customers that this
bar chart does not check, and say where in the project it is checked.

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

# Part E: Gibbs sampling (8 points)

## Question 13 (1 point)

The posterior of $(\lambda, p)$ for one customer is not a standard
distribution. Why could Part E still use a Gibbs sampler? Circle one.

1. With $Z$ added, each full conditional is a standard distribution.
1. The posterior is a gamma times a beta.
1. Gibbs sampling does not need the full conditionals.
1. Customer 1 has only two repeat purchases.

## Question 14 (1 point)

Part E checked the Gibbs sampler against a closed form. Without one, you
could check it by importance resampling: draw $(\lambda, p)$ from the priors
and weight each draw by the likelihood. For which customer would this work
worst? Circle one.

1. A customer with many repeat purchases, like customer 6 with $x = 7$.
1. A customer with no repeat purchases.
1. Customer 1.
1. It works equally well for all of them.

## Question 15 (6 points)

**(i)** (2 points) Explain in words why
$$P(Z = 1 \mid \lambda, p) = \frac{(1 - p)\, e^{-\lambda (T - t_x)}}{p + (1 - p)\, e^{-\lambda (T - t_x)}}$$
gets smaller as $T - t_x$, the time since the last purchase, gets longer.
What do the two terms in the denominator stand for?

\vspace{1.5in}

\newpage

**(ii)** (2 points) At the end of the project, the model predicted about 1.04
holdout purchases per customer with $x = 2$, and they made 1.39. The paper's
equation (10), computed with no simulation at all, also gives 1.04. Is the gap
Monte Carlo error, a mistake in the simulation code, chance in which 214 customers we happened to
observe, or the model? Use the fact that the standard deviation of `x_star`
among these customers is 1.84 ($\sqrt{214} \approx 14.6$).

\vspace{1.8in}

**(iii)** (2 points) Describe one way the model could be wrong that would make
customers with $x = 2$ buy more in the holdout period than it predicts.

\vspace{1.3in}

\newpage

# Part F: Big picture (10 points)

## Question 16 (5 points)

**Choose a sampler.** For each target below, name the method from this module
you would try first, and say in a phrase why. One point each.

1. The Pareto distribution, with $F(x) = 1 - x^{-k}$ for $x \ge 1$.
1. The number of purchases a customer makes in 39 weeks under the full model,
   given `rgamma`, `rbeta` and your `purchases`.
1. A point chosen uniformly in the unit disk, given `runif`.
1. A pair $(\log\lambda, \text{logit}\, p)$ that is bivariate normal with
   correlation 0.3, given `rnorm`.
1. The posterior of $(r, \alpha, a, b)$ given all 2,357 customers, known only
   up to a constant, with no full conditional you can draw from.

\vspace{2.5in}

\newpage

## Question 17 (5 points)

**Find an example.** Point to one place in the practice project that does
each of the following, and say in a phrase what makes it one. One point each.

1. A sampler for a discrete distribution by inversion.
1. A latent variable that is never observed.
1. A sampler that rejects some of its candidates.
1. A process simulated one step at a time, each step given the one before.
1. Checking a Monte Carlo answer against something computed another way.

\vspace{3in}
